locations.name: Brisbane
locations.depot: Port of Brisbane at Fisherman Islands and the Wacol–Richlands industrial corridor
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck or side loader for 40ft and for anything going over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Brisbane. Cargo-worthy and as-is units from the port and Wacol depots, delivered to hill suburbs and industrial yards.
locations.line: Supply is the easy part here. The port is on the doorstep and the depots are strung along the Ipswich Motorway, so you usually get a real choice of grade and size rather than whatever happens to be standing in a yard. The hard part is the last forty metres, because Brisbane is a city of ridges, gullies and old river flats and very few of them give a truck a straight, level run.
locations.uses: lock-up storage on the tight infill blocks going in around Everton Park, Coorparoo and Morningside, parts and trade storage on the industrial land at Wacol, Archerfield and Northgate, somewhere to put a household while a renovation runs three months long, workshop and home-gym conversions tucked in under high-set houses, secure tool storage for builders juggling four sites at once, and feed and machinery storage out on the acreage fringe through Samford and Karana Downs
access: Brisbane is not one delivery job, it is three. The flat industrial belt — Wacol, Richlands, Archerfield, Rocklea, Northgate, Hemmant — is about as good as it gets. Hardstand, wide gates, room to swing a rigid truck and set up, and often a forklift on site already. Those drops get booked and done. The second is the hill country west and north of the river. Paddington, Bardon, Red Hill, Ashgrove, The Gap, Chapel Hill, Kenmore and the streets climbing off Waterworks Road were subdivided long before anybody was thinking about a twelve-metre truck. The driveways are short and pitch away hard at the kerb, so the bed of a tilt-tray touches down before the container has cleared it. The houses are high-set and the only usable ground is underneath or out the back, which makes it a crane job rather than a tilt job. And there is fifty years of fig, poinciana and jacaranda hanging over the road at four metres. Any one of those three is workable on its own. All three at once is why we ask questions before we book a truck. The third problem is ground. From Rocklea through Oxley, Fairfield, Yeronga and along the Breakfast Creek flats the soil is river silt, and silt is a liar. It dries hard, it looks like hardstand, then a wet week goes through it and a corner casting carrying a couple of tonne sinks a hundred millimetres while you stand there watching. The same is true of new fill in the outer estates that has not had a summer on it yet. We would rather lay timber under the castings, or put the container a metre further along on the driveway apron, than leave you with it out of level and a pair of ruts through the lawn. Three photos settle nearly all of this: one from the street looking in, one down the length of the approach, one of the spot itself. Send those and we will tell you which truck is coming before anybody talks about price.

sections.h: Where a Brisbane container comes from, and why that matters
p: Almost every box that ends up in a Brisbane backyard came off a ship at Fisherman Islands and was carted a short distance to a depot at Lytton, Hemmant or out along the Ipswich Motorway through Wacol and Richlands. That short first leg is the whole reason Brisbane buyers get treated well: handling is cheap, turnover is fast, and in any given week there is genuine selection in 20ft rather than a take-it-or-leave-it single unit. If you want a particular grade, a specific door configuration, or a high cube instead of a standard, Brisbane is one of the few places in the country where asking for it is not wishful thinking.

What that does not mean is that every Brisbane address costs the same to get to. A drop at Wynnum or Cleveland is a short run around from the port. A drop at Samford, Dayboro or out past Goodna is a different truck, a different half-day and a different number again, and access at the far end shifts it a third time. We quote the container and the cartage together so there is one figure in front of you and no surprise line waiting on the invoice. Ring with the address and what the container is for, and in most cases that number comes back the same day.

sections.h: Council rules, covenants and where the thing can actually sit
p: The councils across greater Brisbane treat a container on a residential block differently depending on how long it is staying, whether it can be seen from the street, and what you are using it for. Plenty of the newer estates then layer a covenant on top that is stricter than the council position. We are not going to pretend to know the rule for your particular street — it changes, and it is yours to check before you order. The questions worth asking are consistent though: is it temporary or permanent, is it visible from the road, is it storage or a conversion, and does the body corporate or the estate covenant have anything to say about it.

The practical half of that is placement. Behind the building line, screened by a fence or a bit of planting, sitting level and not blocking a drainage path will keep almost everybody comfortable. Parked on the front lawn of a Camp Hill queenslander where the whole street can see it will not. If the plan is to clad it, paint it or build around it, do that thinking before delivery rather than after — shifting a container twenty metres once the truck has left is a second delivery, not an adjustment.

sections.h: Buy it or hire it
p: Hire earns its keep when the need has an end date on it. A renovation with a six-month program, a site store while a build runs, a house being restumped, a deceased estate being worked through. You are not tying up capital in something you will be trying to move on in September, and you are not the one arranging a truck at the far end when you are finished. Buying gets better the moment the timeframe goes vague, because a bought 20ft holds its value here and there is a real second-hand market in Brisbane when you are done with it. The other half of that decision is grade, and it is worth being plain about. Every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, which is what you want if the container is living outdoors and holding anything you would be upset to lose. As-is units cost less and have a genuine place — a site store for steel and formwork, a lock-up for gear that does not mind weather — but they are not sold as watertight and should not be bought as though they are. Tell us what is going inside and how long for, and we will point you at the right one rather than the dearer one.

faqs.q: Can you get a container up a steep driveway in Bardon or The Gap?
faqs.a: Often, but not always with a tilt-tray. Where the driveway pitches down hard off the kerb, the truck bed grounds out before the container is clear, and a short crest halfway up does the same thing. On those blocks we look at a crane truck lifting over the fence or the carport instead, or at a 10ft or 20ft where a 40ft was the original plan. Send a photo taken from the middle of the road looking straight up the drive and we can usually call it on the spot.

faqs.q: How quickly can a container be delivered in Brisbane?
faqs.a: Two to four business days is the normal window from order to on the ground, and it is often quicker for a standard 20ft going to an address with clear access. What stretches it is a crane booking, a unit that has to be moved between depots first, or wet weather on soft ground where waiting two days beats bogging a truck in your yard. If you have a fixed date — a settlement, a site start, a move-out — tell us at the enquiry and we will build the run around it.

faqs.q: Can I see the container before it is delivered to my Brisbane address?
faqs.a: Yes. Our yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley, about an hour west of Brisbane on the Warrego, and the containers sit on hardstand where you can walk around them, open the doors and look down the floor rather than taking anybody's word for the condition. Ring first so somebody is there and the unit you are interested in is accessible. If the drive west is not practical, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery — corners, door end, roof and internal floor.

faqs.q: What size actually fits on a standard Brisbane suburban block?
faqs.a: On a typical 405 to 600 square metre inner or middle-ring block, a 20ft is the sensible ceiling. It is six metres long and needs roughly nine to ten metres of straight run to place, which most side yards and driveway aprons can find. A 40ft on a small block usually means losing the side access entirely and it needs close to twenty metres of clear approach. Where storage volume matters more than footprint, a 20ft high cube gives you an extra 300mm of internal height for the same ground area.

locations.name: Ipswich
locations.depot: our own yard in the Lockyer Valley, about forty minutes west up the Warrego
locations.leadTime: Often next business day, and usually inside two
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft and for tight older streets
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Ipswich, delivered short-haul from our Lockyer Valley yard. Real advice on flood levels, clay ground and street access.
locations.line: Ipswich is one of the few places we can call genuinely short-haul, because the yard is forty minutes west of you up the Warrego rather than the other side of a capital city. That shows up in how fast we can get a truck to you and in what the cartage is worth. What it does not change is the ground and the water, and Ipswich has strong opinions about both.
locations.uses: storage while a Woodend or Sadliers Crossing queenslander gets restumped and reclad, dry lock-up on the new estates at Ripley, Springfield and Redbank Plains where the shed has not been built yet, trade and plant storage across the Carole Park and Wulkuraka industrial land, hay and gear storage on the small holdings out through Rosewood, Marburg and Grandchester, and a secure box to get contents up off the ground and out of a shed that has been through it before
access: The single most useful thing to know about an Ipswich delivery is which part of Ipswich. The newer growth corridor — Springfield Lakes, Ripley, Deebing Heights, South Ripley — is estate country. The streets are narrow by design, cars park both sides, the kerb line is punctuated with stormwater grates and service pits that will not carry a loaded rigid truck's rear axle, and the culs-de-sac have turning circles sized for a garbage truck rather than a tilt-tray with six metres hanging off the back. The other thing about new estates is fill. A block cut and filled eighteen months ago has not settled, the turf is thin over it, and a container corner will find the soft spot for you. The old town is the opposite problem. Woodend, Sadliers Crossing, Eastern Heights and North Ipswich have short pitched driveways, big camphor laurels and figs, low service lines and side gates set out for a wheelbarrow. Plenty of those blocks are perfectly deliverable but need a crane truck rather than a tilt, and that is worth knowing before you order rather than on the morning. Then there is ground. West and south of the river through Rosewood, Marburg, Amberley and Willowbank you get heavy clay that is like concrete in October and like grease in February. On the flats along the Bremer and the Brisbane the soil is silt and old alluvium, which behaves the same way. There are also old coal workings under parts of the district, which is not usually a delivery issue but is worth mentioning to us if your block has known subsidence — we would rather place the container on the firmest part of the site than the most convenient one.

sections.h: Forty minutes down the Warrego
p: Most container sellers quoting an Ipswich job are working out of a depot on the far side of Brisbane, which means the truck runs the Ipswich Motorway both ways and you pay for the whole trip in one form or another. Our yard is at Forest Hill, between Gatton and Laidley, and the run down the Warrego to Ipswich is short, flat and free of city traffic. Practically that means we can often get a container to you the next business day, we can be flexible if the weather pushes a booking, and if you want to come and look at the actual unit first the drive is forty minutes rather than a day out. Ring before you come so somebody is there to walk you round the yard. It also means a second trip is not a disaster. If a delivery has to be pulled at the last minute because a driveway has gone soft, or the container needs to come back and be swapped for a different grade, that is a short run for us rather than a full day's cartage across the city — which is exactly the sort of thing that makes a supplier flexible or inflexible when something goes wrong.

sections.h: What 2011 and 2022 taught people about placement
p: Ipswich floods, and everybody here knows the levels better than any website could tell them. What matters for a container is simple and worth being blunt about: height above the flood line is what protects what is inside it. The container itself is not a flood barrier. Water that reaches the door sill will get past the seals, and an empty container is a very large sealed box that will float and move if the water gets deep enough. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling you something they should not be.

So the useful conversation is about siting. Put it on the highest practical part of the block, not the flattest. Keep it clear of the overland flow path, because in the 2022 event a lot of damage came from water running across blocks rather than from the river backing up. If it is going to be a long-term store on low ground, talk to us about setting it up on blocks or a raised pad so the floor sits higher and the underside stays dry and ventilated. And if you are storing something genuinely irreplaceable, height is worth more than any other single decision you will make about it.

sections.h: Clay, and what the container sits on
p: Reactive clay is the standing feature of the Ipswich district and it moves through the year. It takes up water in summer and swells, then gives it back through winter and shrinks away, and it does not do either evenly across a block. A container placed directly on soil in the dry will settle and rack as that goes on underneath it, and a racked container is a container whose doors stop closing properly. The frame is designed to carry its load through the four corner castings, so once those four points stop being at the same height the whole box starts working against itself. That is the most common complaint we hear about a badly placed unit anywhere in south-east Queensland, it costs nothing to prevent, and it is very expensive to argue with afterwards.

Four hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the corner castings, checked level in both directions, solves almost all of it. Keep the underside clear so air moves and water does not sit. Get the doors on the high side if the ground has any fall, because a container that settles slightly toward the door end goes from easy to open to a two-person job. We will do that levelling as part of the delivery where the site allows it — tell us at the quote if the ground is soft or sloping and we will bring the timber with us.

faqs.q: Is a shipping container safe to use for storage on a flood-prone Ipswich block?
faqs.a: It is a good store, but not because it resists floodwater — it does not. Water that reaches the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty container will float and move if it gets deep enough. What protects your contents is height. Site it on the highest usable part of the block rather than the flattest, keep it out of the overland flow path, and consider setting it on blocks or a raised pad so the floor sits well clear of the ground. Do that and it is a genuinely good long-term store; treat it as a barrier and you will be disappointed at the worst possible moment.

faqs.q: How quickly can you deliver a container to Ipswich?
faqs.a: Faster than most, because our yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley, roughly forty minutes west of Ipswich on the Warrego rather than on the far side of Brisbane. Next business day happens regularly on a standard 20ft with clear access. What slows it down is a crane booking, wet weather on clay where a day's wait beats a bogged truck, or a unit that needs a lockbox or a vent fitted before it goes. Tell us your date at the enquiry — a settlement, a site start, a removalist already booked — and we will build the run around it rather than telling you afterwards that it did not fit.

faqs.q: Can a truck get into a new estate street at Ripley or Springfield?
faqs.a: Usually yes, with a bit of planning. The constraints are consistent across those estates: narrow carriageways with cars parked both sides, service pits and stormwater grates right on the kerb line that will not take a loaded rear axle, and turning circles that are tight for a rigid with a tilt bed. Clearing the parked cars in front of the block for an hour makes the difference on most of them. Send a photo up the street and one of the kerb crossing and we will tell you what we need.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container before buying it from Ipswich?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is an easy trip. The yard is at 24 Forest Hill Fernvale Rd, Forest Hill, just off the Warrego between Gatton and Laidley, with the containers standing on hardstand where you can open the doors and look at the floor. Ring first so the unit you are interested in is accessible and somebody is there to show you through. If the drive does not suit, ask and we will send photos of the actual unit on request before delivery.

locations.name: Gold Coast
locations.depot: Port of Brisbane and the Yatala–Stapylton industrial corridor
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days; add a day where a crane is booked
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where there is side access; crane truck for canal blocks and anything lifted over a house or fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire on the Gold Coast. Canal-front craning, body corporate access and sandy-block delivery handled properly. Give us a call.
locations.line: Getting a container to the Gold Coast is nothing. Getting it onto the block is the whole job. The M1 runs a truck to any postcode from Coomera to Coolangatta without drama, and then you meet a canal-front lot with a two-metre side gate, a body corporate with an opinion, and sand that a truck's rear duals will find the bottom of.
locations.uses: storage for tourism and hire operators who need gear locked away between seasons, site stores on the constant run of knockdown-rebuild jobs from Mermaid to Paradise Point, trade storage on the industrial land at Yatala, Molendinar, Burleigh and Currumbin, event and festival gear that only comes out twice a year, board, bike and boat storage where a garage was never going to be enough, and machinery storage on the hinterland acreage through Currumbin Valley and Tallebudgera
access: The canal blocks are the signature Gold Coast delivery problem. From Sorrento and Broadbeach Waters through Mermaid Waters, Clear Island Waters, Runaway Bay and Hope Island, the lots are wide at the water and narrow at the street, the house fills the width of the block, and there is no side access at all — often not even a gate wide enough for a mower. There is nothing wrong with those sites, they simply are not tilt-tray sites. They are crane sites. A crane truck sets up on the street, lifts the container over the roofline and sets it down in the back yard, and the questions that decide whether it works are all about what is overhead and what is underfoot: power and comms lines across the frontage, palms and figs, and whether the street is wide enough for the outriggers without closing it. Apartments and gated estates bring a different constraint. Body corporate approval, a booked loading dock window, height limits in basements and a building manager who needs notice are all normal, and they are all much easier to sort out a week before delivery than on the day. Then there is sand. The whole coastal strip from Coombabah down to Kirra is sand over a high water table, and dry beach sand carries almost nothing. A loaded truck can sit down to the axles on a nature strip that looked perfectly solid. Behind the strip, the fill in the older canal estates has been sitting for decades and is generally fine, but the newer cut blocks are not. We would rather bring ply or timber and spread the load than pull a truck out of your front lawn. The hinterland is a third case again. Springbrook, Currumbin Valley, Tallebudgera Valley and the Numinbah road are steep, narrow and hard against the bank in places, with low branches and single-lane bridges. A 20ft goes up there comfortably. A 40ft is a conversation.

sections.h: Lifting over the house on a canal block
p: A crane delivery is not exotic on the Gold Coast, it is routine, but it does need more information up front than a tilt-tray drop. What we need to know is the distance from where the truck can legally stand to where the container is going, the height of anything in between — roofline, palms, pergola, pool cage — and whether there are overhead services across the street frontage. A crane truck's reach falls away sharply as the boom goes out, so a container going twenty metres over a two-storey house is a much bigger machine than the same container going eight metres over a fence.

Street width matters as much as reach. The outriggers need firm, level ground and a footprint wider than the truck, which on a narrow canal cul-de-sac can mean temporarily blocking the road. That is manageable with notice and neighbours who know it is happening. The single most useful thing you can do is stand at your front gate, take a photo looking at the house, another looking up at the powerlines, and a third from the back yard toward the street. Those three tell us more than a page of description and they get the job priced properly the first time.

sections.h: Sand, water table and what goes underneath
p: On the coastal strip the container itself is rarely the problem — the ground is. Sand drains beautifully and carries badly, and a container corner casting is concentrating a couple of tonne onto a footprint the size of a dinner plate. Straight onto sand or onto thin turf over sand, it will sink unevenly and the doors will start to bind within a few months. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded level and checked on both diagonals, fix it permanently and cost very little. On blocks with a high water table — which is most of the strip — get the floor a hundred millimetres or more off the ground so air moves underneath and the underside stays dry rather than sitting against damp sand for a decade. The same setup makes it far easier to lift and shift later if you sell the place or reconfigure the yard, because a container that has bedded itself into wet ground has to be dug free before a truck can get near it.

sections.h: Hire that matches a season
p: A lot of Gold Coast demand runs on a calendar. Gear that is needed from September through to Easter and then has to be somewhere secure and dry until the next season. Builders who want a site store for the eight months of a rebuild and not a day longer. Hire operators who scale up over summer and want the storage to scale back down again in June. Event and market traders whose entire business fits in a 20ft between weekends. Hire suits every one of those, because it means you are not carrying an asset through the quiet half of the year and not solving the problem of what to do with it afterwards. It also means the container can be swapped for a bigger or smaller one if the requirement changes, which a purchase does not let you do without selling and buying again.

Buying makes better sense where the container becomes part of how the place works — a permanent store on an industrial lot at Yatala, a workshop out the back of a hinterland block, a lock-up that will still be there in ten years. Every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, which is the grade to be asking for if it is going to live outdoors on the coast permanently. As-is units are cheaper and honest about what they are — they are not sold as watertight, and on a salt-air block that difference will show up sooner than it would inland.

faqs.q: Can you crane a container into a Gold Coast canal-front back yard?
faqs.a: Yes, and on those blocks it is usually the only way, since most canal lots have no usable side access. A crane truck stands on the street, lifts the container over the house and sets it down in the yard. What decides feasibility is reach and clearance: how far the container has to travel horizontally, what height it has to clear, whether there are power lines across your frontage, and whether the street is wide enough for the outriggers. Photos from the gate, the yard and looking up at the lines let us answer properly.

faqs.q: Do I need body corporate approval for a container at a Gold Coast unit complex?
faqs.a: Almost certainly, and it is worth starting that conversation early because approval and a booked delivery window are two separate things. Complexes typically want notice, a nominated time, evidence of insurance from the transport operator, and a route that does not use a basement with a height limit a truck cannot meet. None of that is difficult, but it is very hard to arrange on the morning of delivery. Get the approval in hand first and then let us book a truck around the window you have been given.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into sand on a Gold Coast block?
faqs.a: It will settle unevenly if it is placed straight onto sand or thin turf, because each corner casting concentrates a serious point load. The fix is cheap and permanent: concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded level, so the load spreads. It also keeps the underside off the ground, which matters more here than inland because of the high water table. We will do that levelling on delivery where the site allows — mention the ground type at the quote so we bring the right gear.

faqs.q: Can you deliver up into the Gold Coast hinterland?
faqs.a: Regularly. Springbrook, Currumbin Valley, Tallebudgera Valley, Numinbah and the Tamborine side are all serviced, but the roads change what is sensible. They are narrow, steep in sections, hard against the bank, and there are low branches and single-lane bridges that a long rigid truck has to be driven for rather than simply driven. A 10ft or 20ft goes up there without much fuss. A 40ft needs the approach checked first, and on some of those roads the honest answer is two 20ft instead — which usually gives you more useful space anyway. Send the address and a photo from the road looking at your gate and we will tell you what will make it.

locations.name: Sunshine Coast
locations.depot: Port of Brisbane, run north up the Bruce Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–5 business days; hinterland drops are scheduled around the range run
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck or side loader for 40ft where the approach allows it
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire on the Sunshine Coast, coast to Blackall Range. Straight advice on range roads, sand and acreage delivery access.
locations.line: There are two Sunshine Coasts as far as a truck is concerned, and the boundary is the escarpment. Below it, the flat coastal strip and the growth corridor are straightforward apart from sand. Above it, the range roads to Maleny, Montville and Mapleton decide what size container you can realistically have, and it is better to have that conversation before you order than after.
locations.uses: gear and feed storage on the acreage through Eumundi, Cooroy, Doonan and Belli Park, site stores for the constant build work at Palmview, Aura and Bli Bli, workshop conversions on hinterland blocks where a shed would need approval, secure storage for market and event traders who need everything to disappear between weekends, board and boat storage where the garage lost that argument years ago, and dry storage for small growers and nurseries on the flats
access: Start with the range, because it drives everything above 200 metres. The climbs to Maleny off Landsborough, to Montville off Palmwoods, and to Mapleton off Nambour are narrow, tightly cambered, and stitched with hairpins that a long rigid truck cannot straighten out. There are sections with a rock face on one side and nothing much on the other, weight and length restrictions in places, and mature fig and eucalypt canopy hanging low over the road. A tilt-tray carrying a 20ft handles those climbs. A side loader carrying a 40ft is a genuinely different proposition and on some of those roads the honest answer is no, or two 20ft instead of one 40ft. If the address is up top, ring and settle the size question with us first. Acreage above the range brings the usual rural pattern too: long unsealed driveways with a crown and table drains, gates set at an angle to the road, and turning space at the far end that has to be real rather than optimistic. Decomposed granite and the red volcanic soil up there hold together well in the dry and turn slick in the wet, and the wet lasts longer at altitude than it does on the coast. Below the escarpment the problem is sand and water. Peregian, Coolum, Marcoola, Pelican Waters, Golden Beach and most of the Noosa side are sand over a shallow water table. It looks solid, it carries very little, and a loaded truck will find that out on a nature strip. The canal and lake estates at Pelican Waters, Mooloolaba and Twin Waters add the same no-side-access problem you get on any waterfront lot, which usually means lifting over the fence rather than backing in. Newer estates on the corridor have narrow streets, kerbside parking and service pits that will not take a rear axle. And through summer, a heavy afternoon storm can put a soft block out of action for a day or two.

sections.h: The range decides the size
p: If your address is Maleny, Montville, Flaxton, Mapleton or anywhere along the top of the Blackall Range, the first question is not what you want to store, it is what can physically get there. The roads up were built for a different era of vehicle and they have not got wider. The practical outcome is that a 20ft on a tilt-tray is the workhorse for the range, and it covers most of what people actually need. Where the requirement genuinely is 40ft of length — a workshop, a long-term store on a working block — we look at whether the approach can take a side loader, and if it cannot, two 20ft placed end to end gets you there with more flexibility and an easier delivery.

It is worth saying that this is not caution for its own sake. A truck that cannot make a hairpin has to reverse a long way downhill on a road with no shoulder and a drop on one side, and a container that will not fit through the gate at the top has to go all the way back down again. Both cost a day and neither is anybody's idea of a good time. Five minutes with a satellite image of your driveway and gate, plus a photo taken from the gate looking back toward the road, avoids nearly all of it. If you are on the range and are not sure, ring and describe the approach — we have run enough of those climbs to know which ones are fine and which ones need a different plan.

sections.h: Salt air, sand and setting it up properly
p: On the coastal strip a container will be living in salt air and sitting on ground that drains fast and carries badly. Neither is a problem if the setup is right. Corner pads or hardwood sleepers spread the point load so the unit does not settle out of square and start binding its doors. Keeping the underside off the ground lets air move and stops moisture sitting against the floor bearers. Keeping the roof clear of leaf litter matters more here than most people expect — wet leaves held against a roof panel are what starts surface corrosion, not the sea breeze on its own. The same goes for grass growing up around the bottom rail, which traps moisture against the steel for months at a time. None of this is onerous. A sweep of the roof a couple of times a year, a whipper snipper around the base, and leaving the doors open on a dry day now and then so any condensation clears is the entire maintenance regime, and it is the difference between a container that looks tired in five years and one that is still solid in twenty.

sections.h: Acreage, sheds and the approval question
p: A lot of hinterland and acreage buyers come to us because a container solves a problem a shed does not. It arrives finished, it does not need a slab poured and cured first, it is lockable and vermin-resistant on the day it lands, and it can be moved or sold on later if the plan changes. That combination suits a block that is still being worked out, one where the house is two years away and the tools need to live somewhere in the meantime, or one where a permanent structure means starting a planning process nobody wants to start. It also suits a steep block, because a container can be levelled on pads on ground where a shed slab would mean serious excavation.

Where you do need to be careful is with the rules, which differ between the councils on the coast and depend on how long the container is staying, whether it is visible from the road and whether it is being altered. Estates and rural covenants add their own layer. We will not guess at your particular situation, but the pattern is consistent enough to plan around: temporary and screened is easy, permanent and prominent is where the questions start. Sort that out before delivery rather than after the neighbours have had a look.

faqs.q: Can you get a 40ft container up to Maleny or Montville?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but the range roads are the limiting factor rather than the container. The climbs off Landsborough, Palmwoods and Nambour have tight hairpins, narrow carriageways and low canopy, and a side loader carrying a 40ft cannot always make them safely. A 20ft on a tilt-tray is the reliable option up top. Where you genuinely need the length, two 20ft placed end to end usually delivers more usable, more flexible space and a far simpler delivery. Send us the address and gate photos and we will give you a straight answer.

faqs.q: Will a container sit properly on a sandy Sunshine Coast block?
faqs.a: Yes, provided it is set up on something. Coastal sand from Golden Beach up through Coolum and Peregian drains well but carries poorly, and dropping a container straight onto it means uneven settlement and doors that stop lining up. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, levelled in both directions, solve it for good and keep the underside off a shallow water table. Tell us about the ground when you enquire and we will bring the timber on the truck.

faqs.q: How long does delivery take to the Sunshine Coast?
faqs.a: Two to five business days is normal, with coastal addresses at the shorter end. Hinterland and range deliveries get scheduled around the run up the escarpment, so they can sit a day or two longer, and heavy rain will push a soft or unsealed driveway back rather than risk bogging a truck on your property. If you have a hard date, say so at the enquiry — we would rather build the schedule around it than tell you afterwards that it did not fit.

faqs.q: Can I look at a container before it comes to the Sunshine Coast?
faqs.a: You can. The yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane off the Warrego, and containers sit on hardstand there where you can open the doors and check the floor and the seals yourself. Ring ahead so the unit is accessible. If that drive is not realistic from the coast, ask for photos of the specific container on request and we will send them before delivery, including the corners, the door end and the internal floor.

locations.name: Logan
locations.depot: the Wacol and Yatala industrial corridors either side of Logan
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft and for tight estate frontages
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire across Logan. Narrow new-estate streets, service pits and wide industrial yards — access scoped before the truck rolls.
locations.line: Logan is not one place, it is about seventy of them stitched together, and the delivery ranges from the easiest job of the week to the tightest. A hardstand yard at Crestmead takes ten minutes. A new-estate frontage at Yarrabilba with cars both sides of the road, a service pit on the kerb line and a two-metre gate is a different afternoon entirely.
locations.uses: trade and plant storage across the Crestmead, Berrinba, Slacks Creek and Meadowbrook industrial estates, tool and materials storage for the trades working the estate builds, extra room for growing families on small new-estate lots where the garage went to the cars, gear storage for sporting clubs and community groups, stock overflow for small businesses running out of a home shed, and secure storage on rural-residential blocks around Munruben and Chambers Flat
access: The industrial half of Logan is easy and we will say so. Crestmead, Berrinba, Heathwood, Underwood, Slacks Creek and the Yatala end have wide entries, hardstand, and yards laid out for B-doubles. A container goes in there with no more planning than a phone call. The residential half is where the work is. The newer estates — Yarrabilba, Logan Reserve, Park Ridge, Flagstone, Greenbank — share a set of problems that repeat street after street. The carriageways are narrow and cars park both sides, which leaves a gap a rigid truck cannot get through, let alone stop and set up in. The kerb crossings and nature strips are dotted with stormwater grates, water meters and telecommunications pits that are built for a car and will crack under a loaded rear axle. Turning circles at the end of the culs-de-sac are tight for a truck with six metres of container hanging past the rear axle. And the blocks themselves are cut and filled, so the ground is young — thin turf over fill that has not been through enough wet and dry cycles to settle. The older suburbs bring the opposite. Woodridge, Kingston, Logan Central, Springwood and Daisy Hill have steeper short driveways, older trees and low overhead service lines, and side gates that were set out when the standard mower was narrower. Plenty of those are crane jobs, not tilt jobs. What solves most of it is an hour's notice to the neighbours and three photos: the street looking toward the house, the kerb crossing and nature strip, and the spot itself. Clearing the parked cars in front of the block for that hour is the single biggest thing a customer can do to make a Logan delivery go smoothly.

sections.h: Parked cars, kerbs and pits
p: It sounds trivial until a truck is sitting in your street with nowhere to go. On a typical new-estate frontage there is exactly one usable position for the truck, it is directly in front of your block, and if two cars are parked in it the delivery does not happen — there is nowhere else within reach and no room to turn around and come back at it from the other direction. Neither does it happen if the only way onto the block runs across a telecommunications pit or a stormwater grate, because a loaded rear axle will crack one and the repair becomes the property owner's problem, not the delivery driver's. Those pits are sized for a car crossing them, not twenty tonne stopping on top of one.

None of this is hard to plan around, and almost all of it falls apart only when nobody thinks about it until the morning. We need to know three things: where the truck can legally stand, what it has to cross to get onto the property, and whether there is anything overhead — power, comms, a verandah roof, a mature gum. Give the neighbours an hour's warning, move the cars off the frontage, and tell us at the quote if the kerb crossing has a pit or a grate in it. Where the frontage genuinely will not work, the answer is usually a crane truck lifting from the road over the fence into the yard. It is more machine, but it is less fuss on the day and it goes in first time, which on a tight estate street is worth a great deal more than it costs.

sections.h: Young ground on a new block
p: A cut-and-fill estate block eighteen months old has not finished moving. The turf is thin, the fill underneath is still consolidating, and the drainage across the block is often still being worked out by the landscaping. Drop a container straight onto that and each corner casting punches into it, the unit goes out of square, and within a season the doors need a shoulder. Corner pads or hardwood sleepers, checked level both ways and on both diagonals, cost almost nothing and prevent all of it. If the block has a fall across it, put the door end on the high side so the doors are working with gravity rather than against it. It is also worth thinking about where the container sits relative to the drainage the builder set up — an estate block usually has a designed overland flow path across it, and parking a six-metre steel box in the middle of it will send water somewhere the landscaper did not intend, usually toward the house or the neighbour.

sections.h: Trade storage on the industrial side
p: The other half of what we do in Logan is straightforward commercial work: a lock-up for tools and consumables on a leased industrial lot, a store for stock that will not fit inside the tenancy, a gear store while a build runs on the estates. Those jobs are easy to deliver and the only real decision is whether you want the asset on your books or not. A container on a leased yard is also a useful hedge, because it goes with you when the lease ends rather than being fitout you walk away from.

Hire suits a lease with an end date, a project with a program attached, or a business that is growing and genuinely does not know what it will need in twelve months. Buying suits a permanent fixture on a yard you control or own. If it is going to live outside year-round with stock or tools in it, ask for cargo-worthy — every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. As-is units are cheaper and have a real place on a site where a bit of surface rust and a dent are irrelevant, but they are not sold as watertight, and for anything you need to stay dry that distinction is the whole decision. Tell us what is going in it and we will tell you which one you actually need.

faqs.q: Can a container truck get into a Yarrabilba or Logan Reserve street?
faqs.a: Usually, but the frontage has to be clear. Those estate streets are narrow with cars parked both sides, and a rigid truck with a tilt bed needs a specific stretch of kerb directly in front of your block to set up in. There are also service pits and stormwater grates in the nature strip that will crack under a loaded rear axle. Move the cars for an hour, tell us what the kerb crossing looks like, and most of these go in without drama. Where the frontage genuinely will not work, a crane lift from the road over the fence will, and it is usually the faster option anyway.

faqs.q: What size container fits on a small new-estate block in Logan?
faqs.a: A 20ft is the practical maximum for most estate lots. It is six metres long and needs around nine to ten metres of straight run to place, which the driveway or side yard on a 400 square metre block can generally find. A 40ft usually consumes the entire side access and needs close to twenty metres of clear approach, which those lots rarely have. If you need volume rather than floor length, a 20ft high cube gives an extra 300mm of internal height in the same footprint.

faqs.q: Do I need approval for a container on a residential block in Logan?
faqs.a: It depends on how long it is staying, whether it can be seen from the street and what you are using it for, and many of the newer estates have covenants that are stricter than the council position. We will not guess at the rule for your street — check it before you order. As a rule of thumb, temporary, screened from the road and used for storage is the easy end; permanent, visible and altered is where questions start. Sorting it first is far cheaper than moving it later.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to an industrial yard in Crestmead or Berrinba?
faqs.a: Easily, and it is some of the most straightforward work we do. Those estates have wide entries, hardstand and room to manoeuvre, and there is usually a forklift on site already. Give us the gate address, a contact who will be there, and any site induction requirements before the day. If the yard is shared or has a nominated delivery window, tell us at the booking and we will schedule the run to land inside it rather than turning up at the wrong hour.

locations.name: Jimboomba
locations.depot: the Yatala corridor and our own Lockyer Valley yard
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days; wet weather moves unsealed-driveway drops
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for most acreage drops; crane truck where the gate or the yard is tight
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire around Jimboomba. Acreage delivery done properly: cattle grids, unsealed driveways and horse properties allowed for.
locations.line: Jimboomba is acreage country, and acreage is the friendliest delivery there is right up until it is not. There is space, there is no body corporate and nobody is parking a Corolla where the truck needs to stand. What there is instead is four hundred metres of unsealed driveway, a grid of unknown load rating, and a gate somebody set out for a tractor rather than a rigid truck.
locations.uses: hay, chaff and feed kept dry and away from vermin, tack and rugs stored properly instead of in a leaking shed, tractors, slashers and side-by-sides locked up out of the weather, fencing gear and star pickets in one place instead of four, building materials and tools for owner-builders working on a block with no shed yet, and a secure store on a new acreage purchase where the house is still two years away
access: The cattle grid is the first thing we ask about and the thing most often overlooked. A loaded rigid truck with a container on it is a serious weight concentrated over two axles, and a lot of private grids on rural-residential blocks were built by a previous owner out of whatever rail was available, sized for a ute and a float. There is usually no plate, no rating and nobody who knows. If we cannot establish that a grid will carry the truck, the choices are to use the side gate if there is one, drop at the front and shift the container in with a tractor, or crane it in from a firm stand. All of those work. Driving over a grid and finding out the hard way does not. After that it is the driveway. Four hundred metres of crushed rock or decomposed granite with a crown, table drains either side and a couple of culverts is a comfortable run in the dry. After a wet week the crown greases up, the table drains soften, and a truck that leaves the centre line puts a wheel into a drain and is going nowhere without a tractor. Long driveways also need turning space at the far end that is genuinely truck-sized — a tilt-tray needs room to line up straight before it starts unloading, and reversing four hundred metres out to the road in the dark is nobody's idea of a good afternoon. Then the block itself. Gates that measure narrower than they look. Powerlines running to the house or the pump shed at exactly the wrong height for a lifted bed. Old ironbarks with limbs at four metres. Ground that is hard clay in October and pudding in February. And on horse properties, the simple fact that a truck and a swinging container is not something most horses have seen before.

sections.h: The grid, the gate and the culvert
p: Three pieces of infrastructure decide most Jimboomba deliveries, and all three are easy to check before you order. Measure the gate opening at its narrowest point rather than at the posts — a 20ft container on a tilt bed needs meaningful clearance either side, the bed is wider than you think, and a gatepost that has been clipped by a float once already is not going to survive a truck. Walk the driveway and look at the culverts: a pipe under a fill crossing that has been there thirty years, with grass growing out the end of it and a bit of subsidence over the top, is not one anybody wants to test with twenty tonne. And on the grid, if there is any doubt at all about what it will carry, say so at the enquiry rather than at the front gate on the day.

None of that means we cannot deliver. It means we bring the right truck. Where the driveway or the crossings are the issue, a common answer is to set the container down on firm ground near the road and let you shift it in with a tractor and chains at your own pace, or to bring a crane truck that can stand at the front and place it further in than a tilt could. What we want to avoid is a truck committed to a driveway it cannot back out of.

sections.h: Getting it level, and keeping it that way
p: Acreage ground moves. The clay through this district takes up water through a wet summer and shrinks back hard through the dry months, and it does not do it evenly across a paddock. A container placed straight onto soil will follow that movement, one corner at a time, and it will not go back. A container out of square is a container with doors that will not shut, and the doors are the only part of it you interact with, so it turns a good store into a daily annoyance and then into something you have to pay to fix. The frame is built to carry everything through the four corner castings; the moment those four points stop sitting at the same height the box starts fighting itself.

Four hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the corner castings, dug in level and checked both diagonals, is the whole answer. Get the door end on the high side of any fall so the doors swing with gravity. Keep the grass down around it so air moves and snakes have less reason to be interested, and keep the underside clear of stacked timber and drums so water can get away. Do that on day one and the container will still be sitting square and opening cleanly in fifteen years.

sections.h: Horses, dogs and a truck on the place
p: On a horse property the delivery is as much about the animals as the ground. A tilt-tray unloading makes noise — hydraulics, chains, and a steel box sliding off a steel bed. If there are horses in the paddock the truck has to pass or in a yard nearby, move them before we arrive rather than after the truck is committed to a driveway with no turning space. The same goes for dogs, which are usually more interested in the truck than is good for anybody. Tell us at the booking if there are animals to work around, whether the gates need to stay shut behind us, and if there is a preferred approach that avoids the arena or the laneway. It costs nothing to plan for and it makes the difference between a quiet twenty minutes and a bad day.

faqs.q: Will your truck cross the cattle grid on my Jimboomba driveway?
faqs.a: That depends entirely on the grid, and most private grids out here have no rating plate and no known history. A loaded truck with a container on it puts far more weight through the grid than the ute and float it was probably built for. If you know it is engineered and rated, tell us. If you do not, tell us that too — we will look at using a side gate, setting the container down on firm ground near the road for you to shift in with a tractor, or bringing a crane truck instead. All of those beat finding out mid-crossing.

faqs.q: Can you deliver down a long unsealed driveway?
faqs.a: Regularly, and most of them are fine in the dry. The things that stop us are a soft or greasy surface after rain, table drains that a wheel can drop into, culvert crossings of unknown condition, and no truck-sized turning area at the far end. A tilt-tray needs to line up straight to unload and it should not be reversing hundreds of metres back to the road. Send a photo from the gate looking down the drive and one of the spot with its surroundings and we can plan it properly.

faqs.q: What size container suits an acreage block at Jimboomba?
faqs.a: Space is rarely the constraint out here, so it comes down to what you are storing. A 20ft handles feed, tack, fencing gear and a workshop bench comfortably and is far easier to get down a driveway and through a gate. A 40ft gives you machinery-length storage and suits a working block with good access from the road. Where the driveway is tight but you need the volume, two 20ft placed with a gap between them and a roof across the middle is a common and very useful setup.

faqs.q: Can I inspect the container before it comes out to Jimboomba?
faqs.a: Yes. The yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley, off the Warrego between Gatton and Laidley, and the containers stand on hardstand where you can open the doors, look down the floor and check the seals. Ring first so somebody is there and the unit is accessible. If the drive is not worth it for you, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery — corners, door end, roof and internal floor.

locations.name: Beaudesert
locations.depot: the Yatala corridor, run out along the Mount Lindesay Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days, weather permitting on the back roads
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck where the approach or the yard is tight
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Beaudesert and the Scenic Rim. Creek crossings, unsealed approaches and cattle country access planned in advance.
locations.line: Beaudesert is working country and the containers that go out there work for a living too. The town itself is an easy delivery. It is the country behind it — Kooralbyn, Rathdowney, Christmas Creek, Laravale, the roads climbing toward the border ranges — where the creek crossings, the unsealed approaches and the weather do the deciding, and where a phone call ahead of the truck saves a wasted day.
locations.uses: fodder and hay kept dry through a wet summer, fencing wire, posts and strainers in one lockable place, cattle handling gear and vet supplies stored away from the weather, chemicals and drums secured properly, tools and machinery parts on properties where the shed is full, storage for the small tourism and accommodation operators through the Scenic Rim, and a dry store while a homestead or shed is rebuilt after a storm
access: The defining feature of a Scenic Rim delivery is water crossing a road. The Logan and Albert catchments and their tributaries run through a lot of these properties, and the crossings are frequently low-level causeways rather than bridges. They come up quickly after rain in the ranges — sometimes with no rain at all where you are standing — and they can be over for a day or two afterwards. A crossing with a metre of water is not a maybe for a loaded truck, it is a no. That is not a delay we manufacture; it is the reason we ask about your approach and build a bit of flexibility into rural bookings through the wet. Unsealed approach roads are the second factor. Out toward Christmas Creek, Innisplain, Palen Creek and the Kooralbyn back roads there are long gravel and formed-earth sections that are excellent in the dry and slippery within an hour of a storm, particularly where the surface has been graded recently and not yet had traffic bind it. Add a climb and a camber toward the ranges and a loaded rigid truck loses traction well before an unloaded one does. The ground on the properties themselves splits two ways. The river and creek flats are alluvial soil that carries well when dry and greases badly when wet. Up on the slopes there is rock, basalt scree and ledges under a thin cover, which is firm as anything but rarely level. Both want the container set on pads rather than straight down. Then the ordinary rural details that still stop a truck: gates narrower than they look, grids of unknown rating, cattle on the road, powerlines to the pump shed, and turning room at the far end that has to be big enough for the truck to line up straight before it unloads.

sections.h: Rain moves the date, not the job
p: We would rather ring you and shift a delivery by two days than put a loaded truck across a rising causeway or onto a driveway that has gone to grease. Nobody comes out ahead from a bogged truck — not you, standing there watching it chew a trench across your paddock and wondering who pays for the tractor, and not us, with a driver and a truck tied up for the rest of the day. Through the wet season we build a bit of slack into Scenic Rim bookings for exactly this reason, and we will ring and tell you what is happening rather than leaving you at home waiting on a truck that was never going to make it.

The flip side is that a bit of local knowledge from you is worth a lot. You know which of your crossings goes over first and how long it takes to drop. You know whether the gravel section on your road holds up or turns. Tell us at the booking and we will plan around it. If there is a firm alternative — a neighbour's sealed access, a hardstand near the road, a spot by the shed that stays solid no matter what — that is often the difference between delivering this week and delivering next. It is also worth telling us if there is a window where the road grader has just been through, because a freshly graded surface has no bind in it and will not hold a loaded truck until it has had traffic and a bit of weather on it.

sections.h: Cattle country practicalities
p: On a working property the delivery has to fit around the place rather than the other way round. Gates that need to stay shut behind us, stock that should be moved out of the laneway before a truck comes down it, a grid that may or may not carry twenty tonne, and a preferred approach that avoids the yards during weaning. Tell us all of that when you book and it is a non-event. Leave it until the truck is at the front gate and it becomes a problem for both of us. It is also worth knowing that we can set a container down on firm ground near the road and let you walk it in with a tractor and chains at your convenience — on plenty of properties out here that is the cleanest way to do it.

sections.h: Sitting it on a slope
p: Very little ground around Beaudesert is genuinely level, and a container does not need it to be. What it needs is four corners sitting at the same height. On a slope that means building the low side up — hardwood sleepers stacked and packed, or concrete pads set into the fall — rather than cutting the high side out, which only creates a shelf for water to run along and pond against the container. That distinction gets missed a lot, and it is the difference between a unit that stays dry underneath for twenty years and one that has a wet trench against the bottom rail every time it rains.

Get it right and the container carries its own weight through the corner castings the way it was designed to, the frame stays square and the doors keep swinging cleanly for decades. Get it wrong and the frame racks, the doors bind, and the fix is a lot harder than the prevention. Put the door end on the high side, keep the underside clear so water and air move, and keep the roof free of leaf litter if it is going in under trees. That is the whole maintenance list.

faqs.q: Will you deliver over a creek crossing on a Scenic Rim property?
faqs.a: Yes, when the crossing is passable and the approach is firm. Many of the causeways out through Christmas Creek, Laravale and the Rathdowney side come up fast after rain in the ranges and stay up for a day or two, and a loaded truck does not attempt a crossing with water over it. Tell us at the booking which crossings are on your approach and how they behave, and we will schedule accordingly — or set the container down on firm ground for you to move in with a tractor.

faqs.q: How does wet weather affect delivery to Beaudesert and district?
faqs.a: In town it barely matters. Out on the unsealed roads and long driveways it matters a great deal, because a formed-earth or freshly graded surface goes slick within an hour of a storm and a loaded rigid truck loses traction long before an empty one does. We will ring and move the booking rather than risk bogging a truck on your place. Through summer we plan rural runs with that flexibility built in and keep you updated rather than leaving you guessing.

faqs.q: Can a container be used to store hay and feed on a property here?
faqs.a: It is one of the most common reasons people out this way buy one. A container is lockable, keeps vermin and birds out, and every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, so what goes in dry stays dry. Two things are worth doing: set it on pads so air moves underneath and the floor is not sitting on damp ground, and leave the doors open on a dry day now and then so any condensation clears rather than sitting in there through a humid week.

faqs.q: Can you place a container on sloping ground?
faqs.a: Yes, and most blocks around Beaudesert have some fall. The container does not need level ground, it needs four corners at the same height. We build the low side up with hardwood sleepers or set concrete pads into the fall, rather than cutting into the high side, which only creates a spot for water to sit against the unit. Put the door end on the high side so the doors work with gravity. Done properly on delivery, it stays square and keeps opening cleanly for years.

locations.name: Redlands
locations.depot: Port of Brisbane, a short run around the bay
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days on the mainland; island deliveries are arranged case by case
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, tight bayside blocks and over-fence lifts
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire across the Redlands. Sandy and boggy bayside ground, plus barge access to the bay islands arranged with your quote.
locations.line: The Redlands sit closer to the port than almost anywhere we deliver, so the haul is short and the container is cheap to get to the shire. Everything interesting happens after that: ground that is sand on one street and boggy wetland margin on the next, small bayside blocks with no side access, and a set of islands where the last leg is a barge rather than a road.
locations.uses: boat, trailer, crab pot and fishing gear storage where the garage lost that fight long ago, trade storage for the nursery, turf and landscaping businesses the shire is full of, building materials staged for a job on one of the islands, household storage while a bayside cottage is knocked down and rebuilt, gear storage for schools, clubs and community groups, and dry storage on the acreage pockets out through Mount Cotton and Sheldon
access: Redlands ground is inconsistent over very short distances and that is the thing to get right. Through Victoria Point, Redland Bay, Thornlands and Wellington Point you get sandy profiles that drain fast and carry poorly — a loaded truck's rear duals will sit down into a nature strip that looked entirely solid. A street or two away, behind the bay and around the melaleuca and paperbark margins, the ground is low, holds water and stays soft long after the surface looks dry. Neither is a reason not to deliver; both are a reason to know before the truck is on the block. The blocks themselves tend to be modest, particularly the older bayside stock at Cleveland, Ormiston and Wellington Point. Houses sit close to one boundary, the side gate is narrow, and there are big established gums and figs with limbs right where a lifted tilt bed wants to be. Overhead service lines across the frontage are common. On plenty of those, lifting over the fence with a crane truck is quicker and safer than trying to thread a tilt-tray down the side. The newer estates at Thornlands and Redland Bay have the usual pattern: narrow streets, cars parked both sides, service pits and stormwater grates on the kerb line that will crack under a loaded axle, and fill that has not settled. The islands are their own thing. North Stradbroke and the southern Moreton Bay islands — Russell, Macleay, Lamb, Karragarra — are reached by barge, which means the delivery has a marine leg with its own constraints on vehicle size, weight and loading. Island roads are often unsealed, narrow and short on turning space, and the blocks are frequently sandy. It is all doable, we do it, and it needs to be arranged rather than simply booked.

sections.h: Getting a container onto a bay island
p: Island deliveries work, and they are one of the more common questions we get from the Redlands. The container travels by road to the ramp and then across on a barge, and the barge is what shapes everything else about the job. Barge operators set their own limits on vehicle length and weight, their own loading arrangements and their own running times, and those are theirs to set rather than ours to promise. We deliberately do not publish a schedule or a fixed arrangement here, because it changes and a website that is six months out of date on a barge booking will cost you a day standing at a ramp.

What we will do is work it out with you and the operator as part of the quote, so you get one answer covering the container and getting it to your block rather than a container price and a shrug about the water. Practically, a 20ft is far easier to move onto an island than a 40ft, and on Russell, Macleay, Lamb and Karragarra the island roads and blocks make that even more true. Tell us the island, the street and what the block looks like at the enquiry and we will come back with something real.

sections.h: Sand one street, bog the next
p: The practical version of the Redlands ground problem is that you cannot judge it from the footpath. Sandy blocks look firm and are not, low blocks look dry on top and are wet 200mm down, and both will let a corner casting sink unevenly within a season. The answer either way is the same and it is cheap: concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded and levelled in both directions, so the point load spreads and the underside stays off the ground.

It matters here more than in most places because of the water table. A container floor sitting hard against damp ground never gets a chance to dry out underneath, and that is where trouble starts on a long-term store — not from the roof, from below. Get it a hundred to a hundred and fifty millimetres up with air moving under it and the difference over ten years is considerable, both in the condition of the underside and in how easy it is to lift the thing out again if you ever need to. Tell us what the ground is like when you enquire — sandy, low and wet, filled, or a proper slab — and we will bring the right materials on the truck and do the levelling as part of the delivery rather than leaving you with a job to sort out afterwards.

sections.h: Salt air and a bit of upkeep
p: A shipping container spent its working life crossing oceans, so salt air is not new to it, but a container parked in a bayside back yard is in a different situation to one on a ship: it sits still, under trees, with leaf litter collecting on the roof and grass growing up around the base. Wet leaves held against a roof panel and long grass trapping moisture against the bottom rail are what actually start surface corrosion, far more than the sea breeze does. Keep the roof swept, keep the grass down around the base, keep the underside clear and open, and leave the doors open on a dry day occasionally so any condensation clears. That is essentially the whole maintenance list, and it is the difference between a unit that looks tired in five years and one that is still solid in twenty.

faqs.q: Can you deliver a container to North Stradbroke or the southern Moreton Bay islands?
faqs.a: Yes. The container travels by road to the ramp and crosses on a barge, and the barge operator sets the limits on vehicle size, weight and loading times. We arrange that leg with them as part of your quote rather than quoting the road portion and leaving you to sort out the water. A 20ft is considerably easier to get onto an island than a 40ft, and the island roads and blocks usually reinforce that. Give us the island, the street and a description of the block and we will come back with a real answer.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into sandy ground in the Redlands?
faqs.a: It will settle unevenly if it goes straight onto sand or thin turf, because each corner casting concentrates a large point load into a small footprint. Low, boggy blocks behind the bay do the same thing for the opposite reason. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded level, solve it permanently and keep the floor clear of a shallow water table. Mention the ground type at the enquiry and we will bring the materials and level it on delivery rather than leaving you to it.

faqs.q: There is no side access at my Cleveland house. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Usually yes, with a crane truck lifting from the street over the fence or the house into the back yard. That is routine on the older bayside blocks where the house sits close to a boundary and the side gate is narrow. What decides it is reach and clearance — how far the container has to travel horizontally, what height it must clear, whether there are service lines across the frontage, and whether the street gives room for the outriggers. Photos from the gate, from the back yard and looking up at the lines let us answer quickly.

faqs.q: Which grade should I buy for a container living outdoors near the bay?
faqs.a: For anything that has to stay dry long-term in salt air, cargo-worthy is the grade to ask for — every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. As-is units are cheaper and perfectly useful where a bit of surface rust or a dent does not matter, but they are not sold as watertight and that will show up sooner in a coastal position than it would inland. Tell us what is going inside it and we will tell you honestly which grade you need.
